headline: Race and Gut bass smash swim shads as 68-degree water stacks bait
subhead: Big stripers crush butterfish and squid in the rips while bluefish wreck everything else.
body_markdown:
The eastern Sound is absolutely on fire right now, and it's all about water temperature and bait positioning. We hit 68 degrees this week — that magic number that turns The Race and Plum Gut from decent fishing into a feeding frenzy. The thermocline is setting up perfectly at 45 feet, stacking butterfish and squid against the structure, and the bass are responding like they should.

I've been running three-way rigs with 8-ounce cannonballs and 80-pound leaders to keep the presentations clean in the screaming current. But here's the kicker — swim shads are absolutely destroying bucktails on size. I'm talking 7-inch Tsunami swim shads producing multiple overslot bass while the same bucktail that usually crushes them is only pulling slot fish. The bigger profile in that heavy current is triggering the gorilla bass that are keyed on the thick butterfish schools.

The Race has been the star performer. Water's running 3 to 4 knots on the big moon tides, and you need to time it right. I'm fishing the last two hours of the ebb when the rip stands up but isn't completely evil. The bass are stacked from 80 feet down to 40 feet across the main structure, and they're aggressive. Had seven bass to 37 inches yesterday morning, kept one slot fish and released the rest. The key is following that bottom contour and taking preemptive cranks as you drift from deep to shallow — lose contact with bottom in that current and you're done.

Plum Gut is producing similar action but with more boat pressure. The flood tide has been better there, especially the first hour when the current starts pushing but hasn't reached full scream. Same rig setup — heavy three-way with that stiff 80-pound leader to stand the bait off bottom. The bluefish have moved in too, and they're wrecking expensive lures. Use wire or heavy fluorocarbon if you're throwing plugs.

Bait situation is interesting. The butterfish showed up early this year, which is unusual, and they're thick in the 40 to 60-foot zone. Squid are scattered through the eastern Sound, particularly around Fishers Island and moving into the rips. The bass are feeding heavily on both, which explains why the bigger swim shads are outproducing traditional bucktails — they match the butterfish profile perfectly.

Current speed is critical. When it's ripping at 4-plus knots, the fishing shuts down. But in that 2 to 3-knot sweet spot, the bass feed aggressively. I'm using the double-drop method — hit bottom, crank twice, drop again to remove the belly, then work the bait. The Humminbird is showing fish marks consistently, and when you see them stacked on the screen, drop fast and get ready.

Weakfish are starting to show in the mix too. Nothing huge yet, but a few 16 to 18-inch fish are coming over the rail with the bass. They're hitting the same presentations, just lighter bites.

Sea bass action has been solid in the deeper structure around Fishers Island. The 55-foot drops are holding good numbers, though you're sorting through plenty of shorts to find keepers. Bucktails and jigs in the 3 to 6-ounce range are getting it done.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon Friday which means spring tides and serious current. The Race will be unfishable at peak flow, but the edges and the slack periods should be dynamite. That new moon will also push more bait out of the back bays, and I expect the bass fishing to get even better. Water temps should hold in the mid to upper 60s, keeping that thermocline tight and the bait concentrated.

The eastern Sound is fishing as well as I've seen it in years. Get out there with heavy tackle, swim shads, and patience for the current. When it all comes together, you'll understand why we put up with the boat traffic and the challenging conditions.
